summary: Introduces a 6to4 anycast address so 6to4 routers can find relays without manual setup, and defines how relays use it and advertise its prefix. It also records IANA's reservation. This document is historic and was replaced by RFC 7526.

plainLanguage.summary: Instead of asking for a particular helper's address, you call one shared number and the nearest helper answers. This is for 6to4 relays. It is now historic and was replaced.

questions: how do 6to4 routers find a relay
subtitle: One well-known IPv4 prefix lets 6to4 routers find the nearest relay to the IPv6 Internet without manual setup.

tldr.problem: A small network using 6to4 needs a default route to reach the native IPv6 Internet, but finding one is a hurdle, and a route found by hand often points to a router on the far side of the Internet with poor performance.
tldr.mechanism: The memo reserves one IPv4 prefix, 192.88.99.0/24, that 6to4 relay routers advertise. 6to4 routers send their IPv6 default route to the matching 6to4 address, and normal IPv4 routing delivers packets to the nearest relay.
tldr.outcome: The document is now Historic and was replaced by RFC 7526.

today: RFC 3068 is Historic and was obsoleted by RFC 7526, so it should not be treated as a current specification. It builds on RFC 3056.

sections.title: The Default Route Problem
sections.content:
RFC 3056 describes two ways to run a 6to4 routing domain. If the domain uses an IPv6 exterior routing protocol, its routers learn routes to all IPv6 networks. If not, each 6to4 router using a given relay router has a default IPv6 route pointing at that relay.

The second case is typical for small networks, and the RFC says finding and configuring that default route is a significant hurdle. Even when a route is found, it often points to a router on the other side of the Internet, which gives very poor performance.

This memo proposes a standard way to define the default route, so that configuration is automatic, the nearest relay is found automatically, and traffic moves to another relay if one fails.
sections.plainLanguage: Small networks had to hunt for the right helper to reach the IPv6 world, and often found one very far away. This memo gives everyone one easy address that leads to a nearby helper.

sections.title: The Anycast Prefix and Address
sections.content:
The memo adds a few definitions on top of RFC 3056. The 6to4 Relay anycast prefix is the IPv4 prefix 192.88.99.0/24. The 6to4 Relay anycast address is host number 1 in that prefix, 192.88.99.1.

The 6to4 IPv6 relay anycast address is derived from it by the 6to4 rules, using a null prefix and a null host identifier: 2002:c058:6301::.

Each relay also has an equivalent IPv4 unicast address, a regular IPv4 address for that one router. Packets sent to it are treated as if they had been sent to the anycast address, which makes it possible to address a specific relay for testing.
sections.plainLanguage: There is one shared address for the whole group of helpers, and each helper also keeps a private address of its own so you can check on it individually.

sections.title: How Routers and Relays Behave
sections.content:
A 6to4 router is configured with the IPv6 default route ::/0 pointing to the 6to4 IPv6 anycast address. Packets for that route are tunneled in IPv4 to the address taken from the route.

A relay that follows this memo advertises the anycast prefix in the IGP of its IPv4 autonomous system, as if it were a connection to an external network. It then receives packets bound to the anycast address and relays them to the IPv6 Internet as RFC 3056 specifies. Each such relay MUST also provide an equivalent IPv4 unicast address.

An AS that wants neighbors to use its relays advertises the prefix in the EGP. With BGP, the initial AS path must contain the announcing AS number. The RFC suggests putting the router's equivalent IPv4 address in the BGP aggregator attribute, but says further work is needed on this point. To IPv4, the whole IPv6 network then looks like one multi-homed network with many access points.
sections.plainLanguage: Each helper announces that it can be reached at the shared address. The network then sends your message to whichever announcing helper is nearest.

sections.title: Monitoring, Failover and Access Control
sections.content:
Anycast has a known cost: the sender does not see which relay got its packets, so a transient failure is hard to pin on one router. The RFC therefore requires that a relay include a monitoring function and that it stop injecting the anycast route immediately if the relay function is not operational. When it does, the local IGP computes a route to the next best relay.

For fault isolation, a domain manager first retrieves the equivalent unicast IPv4 address of the router the user is hitting, from the IGP tables or from EGP data such as BGP path attributes, and then runs connectivity tests against that address. The equivalent address can also feed a centralized monitoring function, for example by tunneling a test IPv6 packet through it.

Only ASes that run relays and are willing to serve the IPv6 network announce the prefix. They can use existing peering and transit agreements to decide who may use the service, and possibly to charge for it.
sections.plainLanguage: If a helper breaks, it must stop saying it is available, and the network quietly switches to the next nearest one. Helpers also keep a private address so people can test each one.

sections.title: Design Questions and Future Work
sections.content:
The RFC answers several concerns raised in the NGTRANS working group. A whole /24 is used rather than a single address because many default-free networks filter out routes that are too specific, such as anything smaller than a /24. A separate AS number for all relays, suggested in an early version, turned out not to be needed for practical operation.

The memo argues the scheme scales, since a few relays can start and more ISPs can add relays as IPv6 demand grows. It also argues the scheme does not trap networks in transition, because easy connectivity builds trust in moving to real IPv6 addresses.

One drawback is left for further study: a default route may lead to a relay that is not on the most direct path to the target. A possible fix is a redirection procedure by which the 6to4 router learns the best route for a specific destination.
sections.plainLanguage: People asked whether one big shared address wastes space or keeps everyone stuck in the old way. The author says no to both, and admits the nearest helper is not always the best one.

sections.title: Security and IANA
sections.content:
The generic risks of 6to4 tunneling are covered in RFC 3056. The anycast technique adds one more: a rogue router or rogue AS could announce a bogus route to the anycast prefix and divert traffic. IPv4 network managers must protect the integrity of their routing to this prefix much as they do for IPv4 routing in general.

On the IANA side, the memo documents the allocation by IANA of an IPv4 prefix dedicated to 6to4 gateways to the native IPv6 Internet. No recurring assignment is needed.
sections.plainLanguage: A bad actor could pretend to be the nearest helper and steal your messages, so network managers must guard against fake announcements.
